newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Facts about Algeria's parliamentary election.
newsitem.headline: Facts about Algeria's parliamentary election.

text.p: Algerians voted on Thursday in parliamentary elections in which 39 political parties and hundreds of independent candidates were running for the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house).
Here are main details on the voting:

ELECTORATE - Total of 16.77 million people were eligible to vote, including 7.6 million women. Voting is not compulsory. More than 338,000 new voters can take part, having reached the minimum voting age of 18. Expatriate voters, numbering 743,237, began voting last weekend in embassies and consulates and continued through Thursday.

POLLING STATIONS - There are 37,587 polling stations in the country's 48 main cities and 1,500 small towns and villages and 5,273 so-called itinerant (mobile) voting stations in remote areas mainly in the south. The government mobilised 400,000 employees to staff the polling.
VOTING HOURS - 8 a.m (0700 GMT) to 7 p.m (1800 GMT) but local authorities may extend polling hours to help voters.

Army and security forces voted two days earlier to be free to protect voters against Moslem guerrillas who have been trying since 1992 to topple the government. About 60,000 people have died in the conflict.
Bedouins, scattered in desert and mountain areas, started voting 72 hours ahead of Thursday's mainstream vote.
TURNOUT AND RESULTS - Partial turnout figures were to be given every few hours, most likely from 10 a.m. (0900 GMT). Final results were likely on Thursday night or Friday morning.

CANDIDATES - A total of 7,196 candidates were running under 39 party flags and 553 were competing as independents. The outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was barred. A total of 322 woman candidates, or 4.2 percent, were standing.
Candidates must gather at least five percent of votes in a constituency to be elected. The number of seats are allotted proportionally between contending candidates following their respective scores.

SEATS - Three hundred and eighty seats were at stake, including eight for Algerian expatriates. The capital Algiers has most seats, 24, followed by the eastern region of Setif with 16. Other constituencies have between four and 10 seats.

COUNTING PROCEDURE - Local election officials, watched by candidates' representatives, were to count votes inside the polling stations and pass them to the interior ministry heaquarters for official release.

MONITORING - An independent election commission, headed by former nationalist leader Salah Boubnider and with representatives of 21 political parties, supervised the poll. More than 250 officials from the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and the Arab League, were also monitoring the voting.
